parts:
Ainars:

The short answer to your question is the predicted values you are
looking at are estimated densities not estimated abundances; if you wish
to alter those cell-specific values to abundances, multiply them by
cell-specific areas. We made the decision to place density estimates
into the Distance database, we opted to use densities and let the user
alter them to abundances if they wished. That is why altering cell area
does not change those values, but does change reported abundance. Sorry
this is not well documented.

messages.subject: Re: Problems with predicted abundance values in DSM
parts:
Thanks Eric,

This explains why predicted values are so much smaller than I expected, but
it does not solve a problem. Even taking into account that these are
densities they are still too small.
I assume the predicted densities are given as birds per square meter (the
area unit that I have tried to use consistently in the Distance). So by
multiplying with grid cell area (1 million square meters) I should get
abundances for each grid square (= densities per sq km). However, now the
values are in range from 0 to 10.5. Thus they seem to be ca 100 times
smaller than expected (size of largest observed flocks in the dataset were
up to 3000 birds). Of course, I do not expect the predicted values to match
observed values, but I expected them to be more or less in the same range.
Now the obtained density values look more like observation densities (not
bird densities). Only less than 1000 out of 16500 grid cells have values
above 2 and less than 70 cells have values above 5.
Regarding the total abundance values predicted by DSM engine - they also are
much smaller than predictions done by MRDS, MCDS or CDS engines. For
example, for the same data MRDS predicts 275583 (from 228662 to 332133)
birds while DSM predicts only 6884 birds which is much less than actually
counted (97812 birds in 1623 detections).
So almost all the concerns of my previous post still remain.
Can it be that I have forgot to set correct area or distance units
somewhere? (I have set correct units and have data in correct units in Data
browser fileds, Survey methods and data Properties, Data filter properties
and Grid cell area of the Prediction tab of the Model definition properties.
Are there any other places to check?) What else could I have done wrong?
Any suggestions are very welcome.

best wishes
Ainars

messages.author: adcf3e83b7a00594
messages.subject: Re: Problems with predicted abundance values in DSM
parts:
Dear Ainars

First of all, I am not native-english speaking so I'm sorry for my englis=
h.
I had similar problem as you, but in the oposite way: In one of my=20
surveys, I obtained a ridiculous large number of animals, so I had to=20
investigate the case. I found a similar question in this list, and an=20
answer of Dr. Charles Paxton (I will copy for you bellow) that I think=20
is a good point. The problem could be number of knots of splines in GAM=20
models. If you let free knots (default is 10 for every predictor=20
variable), may be you can obtain a very good model in terms of deviance=20
explained but a very poor in terms of predictive capacity. This make=20
sense, because as more knots (more degrees of freedom) you have in you=20
model, your curve follow your data perfectly, but only your data,=20
probably you can say little about other situations (predictions). So, I=20
followed suggestions of Charles, and I established a maximun number of=20
knots for my predictor variables (for pure spatial Lat and Long I=20
established k=3D5 as max, for the other, only k=3D4). It works for me ver=
y=20
well. I hope can help you.

best wishes
Natalia Schroeder

Hi List,

Personally I think the maximum number of degrees of freedom allowed
to a potential explanatory variable should reflect how plausibly
bendy the analyst thinks the relationship could be. The default for
gams is 10 knots, 9 degrees of freedom. Is the response of whales say
to depth for example really likely to be a curve that uses 9 degrees
of freedom? I typically constrain my curves to a maximum of 5 or 6
knots, perhaps more if some purely spatial variable like Lat or Lon
is being used but never now the gam default of 10. This can be
implemented as s(Depth,k=3D5) in writing the model formula. This still
gives considerable flexibility.

thanks
Charles

Dr. Charles Paxton

Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling

University of St Andrews
The Observatory
Buchanan Gardens
St Andrews
Fife KY16 9LZ

parts:
Dear Natalia,

Thank you for the suggestion.
Yes, I was aware of this possible overfitting issue. In my formulas all=20
covariates except X and Y coordinates had k=3D4 setting.
I just tried very simple formula such as ~te(x.coord, y.coord, k=3D5) +=20
s(depth, k=3D4) for several species (i.e. using different data filters) a=
nd=20
consistently got very low predicted values (ca 50 times lower than=20
corresponsing estimates using MRDS engine and also much lower than actual=
=20
observations). Changing k setting and including/removing additional=20
covariates did not have big effect on predicted total abundance (+/-30 bi=
rds=20
compared to initial model).
So I tend to think that problem is not in the formula. It could rather be=
in=20
some configuration setting or wrong measurement unit somewhere. Actually =
I=20
have no idea how to proceed from this point within Distance framework.

best wishes
Ainars Aunins

-----Original Message-----=20
From: Schroeder Natalia
Sent: Monday, August 20, 2012 7:58 PM
To: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Problems with predicted abundance values in DSM

Dear Ainars

First of all, I am not native-english speaking so I'm sorry for my englis=
h.
I had similar problem as you, but in the oposite way: In one of my
surveys, I obtained a ridiculous large number of animals, so I had to
investigate the case. I found a similar question in this list, and an
answer of Dr. Charles Paxton (I will copy for you bellow) that I think
is a good point. The problem could be number of knots of splines in GAM
models. If you let free knots (default is 10 for every predictor
variable), may be you can obtain a very good model in terms of deviance
explained but a very poor in terms of predictive capacity. This make
sense, because as more knots (more degrees of freedom) you have in you
model, your curve follow your data perfectly, but only your data,
probably you can say little about other situations (predictions). So, I
followed suggestions of Charles, and I established a maximun number of
knots for my predictor variables (for pure spatial Lat and Long I

established k=3D5 as max, for the other, only k=3D4). It works for me ver=
y

well. I hope can help you.

best wishes
Natalia Schroeder

Hi List,

Personally I think the maximum number of degrees of freedom allowed
to a potential explanatory variable should reflect how plausibly
bendy the analyst thinks the relationship could be. The default for
gams is 10 knots, 9 degrees of freedom. Is the response of whales say
to depth for example really likely to be a curve that uses 9 degrees
of freedom? I typically constrain my curves to a maximum of 5 or 6
knots, perhaps more if some purely spatial variable like Lat or Lon
is being used but never now the gam default of 10. This can be
implemented as s(Depth,k=3D5) in writing the model formula. This still
gives considerable flexibility.

thanks
Charles

Dr. Charles Paxton
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St Andrews
The Observatory
Buchanan Gardens
St Andrews
Fife KY16 9LZ
